samples.summary: `refusalMessage` uses a `default:` branch instead of an exhaustive switch over `RangeOpRefusal`, so any refusal reason added later silently gets the autofill copy ("Can't autofill across merged cells") with no compile error. Since the whole point of the change is that a refusal explains itself, an exhaustive switch (case 'merge-autofill' + a `never` assertion / throw) fits the design better and keeps `tsc` as the guard when the union grows.
samples.evidence: switch (refusal) { case 'merge-source-split': ... case 'merge-dest-partial': ... default: return "Can't autofill across merged cells. Unmerge them first."; }

samples.summary: A fourth same-class silent merge refusal is left uncovered by the new channel: `Sheet.sortFilterByColumn` returns `false` when the filter rows intersect a merged block (packages/sheets/src/model/worksheet/sheet.ts:3448-3450) with the same "looks like the gesture did nothing" symptom the task describes. The new type is named `RangeOpRefusal` (a generic range-gesture refusal) and the design doc now advertises the reporting path, so the sort refusal reads as an inconsistency in the mechanism. The issue's acceptance criteria name only drag-move and autofill, so this is a consistency gap rather than an unmet criterion.

One channel carries two names: the model calls it a "refusal" (`RangeOpRefusal`, `setOnRefusal`) while the view/host calls it a "notice" (`setOnNotice`, `Spreadsheet.onNotice`), and the frontend renders every notice as `toast.error`. A generic `onNotice` name invites non-error notices later that would still surface as red toasts; naming the host hook after what it carries (e.g. `onRefusal`/`onGestureRefused`) or documenting that the channel is error-severity only would keep the layering legible. Purely a naming preference — the shape matches the neighbouring `onValidationError` hook the task pointed at.
samples.evidence: public onNotice(callback: (message: string) => void): void { this.worksheet.setOnNotice(callback); }
